To start, set the decimal equal to a variable. Multiply the decimal by 10 and subtract the original decimal from it. Finally, divide both sides by 9 to obtain the fractional form of the decimal. For example, 0.7 repeating would be 7/9, and 1.2 repeating would be 11/9. |
| Converting repeating decimals to fractions (part 2 of 2) | [link](https://www.khanacademy.org/math/cc-eighth-grade-math/cc-8th-numbers-operations/cc-8th-repeating-decimals/v/coverting-repeating-decimals-to-fractions-2) | [Ihws0d-WLzU](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ihws0d-WLzU) | Repeated decimals can be converted into fractions by shifting the decimal to the right and subtracting the decimals. To do this, multiply the number by 10 to the second power, then subtract. For example, 0.363636 repeating is 4/11 and 0.7141414 repeating is 707/990. Another example is 3.257257257 repeating, which is 3254/999. This calculation can be done in the head or by borrowing. After the subtraction, the numerator and denominator can be reduced and the fraction can be simplified. |

If we can solve the equation and get something like x=b where b is a specific number, then we have one solution. If we end up with a statement that's always false, like 3=5, then there's no solution. If we end up with a statement that's always true, like 5=5, then there are infinite solutions. |

| Systems of equations with substitution: potato chips | [link](https://www.khanacademy.org/math/algebra/x2f8bb11595b61c86:systems-of-equations/x2f8bb11595b61c86:solving-systems-of-equations-with-substitution/v/solving-systems-with-substitution) | [2EwPpga_XPw](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2EwPpga_XPw) | To solve a system of equations using substitution... 1. Isolate one of the variables in one of the equations, e.g. rewrite 2x+y=3 as y=3-2x. 2. You can now express the isolated variable using the other one. *Substitute* that expression into the second equation, e.g. rewrite x+2y=5 as x+2(3-2x)=5. 3. Now you have an equation with one variable! Solve it, and use what you got to find the other variable. |

So all we need to do is check each interval that is between two consecutive zeros (or before the smallest zero and after the largest zero). |
| Multiplicity of zeros of polynomials | [link](https://www.khanacademy.org/math/algebra2/x2ec2f6f830c9fb89:poly-graphs/x2ec2f6f830c9fb89:poly-intervals/v/polynomial-zero-multiplicity) | [jrFLb9ZoZH0](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jrFLb9ZoZH0) | The polynomial p(x)=(x-1)(x-3)² is a 3rd degree polynomial, but it has only 2 distinct zeros. This is because the zero x=3, which is related to the factor (x-3)², repeats twice. This is called multiplicity. It means that x=3 is a zero of multiplicity 2, and x=1 is a zero of multiplicity 1. Multiplicity is a fascinating concept, and it is directly related to graphical behavior of the polynomial around the zero. |

This approach helps us overcome the indeterminate form and find the limit, showcasing the power of trig identities in solving limit problems. |

#### Estimate limit values from graphs

| Title | Khan Academy | YouTube | Summary |

| Estimating limit values from graphs | [link](https://www.khanacademy.org/math/ap-calculus-ab/ab-limits-new/ab-1-3/v/limits-from-graphs) | [mols6pMKrto](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mols6pMKrto) | In this video, we learn to estimate limit values from graphs by observing the function's behavior as x approaches a value from both left and right sides. If the function approaches the same value from both sides, the limit exists. If it approaches different values or is unbounded, the limit doesn't exist. |
| Examining unbounded limits | [link](https://www.khanacademy.org/math/ap-calculus-ab/ab-limits-new/ab-1-3/v/unbounded-limits) | [56qtGRCd8bE](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=56qtGRCd8bE) | This video discusses estimating limit values from graphs, focusing on two functions: y = 1/x² and y = 1/x. For y = 1/x², the limit is unbounded as x approaches 0, since the function increases without bound. For y = 1/x, the limit doesn't exist as x approaches 0, since it's unbounded in opposite directions. |
| Estimating one-sided limits from graphs | [link](https://www.khanacademy.org/math/ap-calculus-ab/ab-limits-new/ab-1-3/v/one-sided-limits-from-graphs) | [nOnd3SiYZqM](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nOnd3SiYZqM) | A one-sided limit is the value the function approaches as the x-values approach the limit from *one side only*. For example, f(x)=\|x\|/x returns -1 for negative numbers, 1 for positive numbers, and isn't defined for 0. The one-sided *right* limit of f at x=0 is 1, and the one-sided *left* limit at x=0 is -1. |
| Estimating one-sided limits from graphs: asymptote | [link](https://www.khanacademy.org/math/ap-calculus-ab/ab-limits-new/ab-1-3/v/one-sided-limits-from-graphs-asymptote) | [5f1-Rg3MmKs](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5f1-Rg3MmKs) | This video explores estimating one-sided limit values from graphs. As x approaches 6 from the left, the function becomes unbounded with an asymptote, making the left-sided limit nonexistent.
